'''''Lavandula angustifolia''''', formerly ''L. officinalis'', is a [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Lamiaceae]], native to the [[Mediterranean basin]]. Its common names include '''lavender''', '''true lavender''' and '''English lavender'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=LAAN81|taxon=Lavandula angustifolia|access-date=23 January 2016}}</ref> (though it is not native to England); also '''garden lavender''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''common lavender''' and '''narrow-leaved lavender'''.

==Description==

It is a strongly aromatic [[shrub]] growing as high as {{convert|1 to 2|m|ft|frac=2}} tall. The [[leaves]] are [[evergreen]],  {{convert|2|-|6|cm|frac=2|abbr=off}} long, and {{convert|4|-|6|mm|in|frac=16}} broad. The flowers are typically purple (lavender-coloured), produced on spikes {{convert|2|-|8|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} long at the top of slender, leafless stems {{convert|10|-|30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long.{{Citation needed|date=October 2024}}

==Etymology==
The [[species]] name ''angustifolia'' is Latin for "narrow leaf".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lavandula angustifolia - Plant Finder |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=281393&isprofile=1&gen=Lavandula |access-date=2024-10-28 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref> Previously, it was known as ''Lavandula [[officinalis]]'', referring to its medicinal properties.

==Cultivation==
English lavender is commonly grown as an [[ornamental plant]]. It is popular for its colourful flowers, its fragrance, and its ability to survive with low water consumption. It does not grow well in continuously damp soil and may benefit from increased drainage. It does best in [[Mediterranean climate]]s similar to its native habitat, characterised by wet winters and dry summers. It is fairly tolerant of low temperatures, and is generally considered hardy to [[Royal Horticultural Society]] zone H6, or [[USDA]] [[Hardiness zone|zone 5]].<ref name=usdaphz>[http://www.usna.usda.gov/Hardzone/ushzmap.html ''USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120704232205/http://www.usna.usda.gov/Hardzone/ushzmap.html |date=2012-07-04 }}. Retrieved on 2008-05-22.</ref> It tolerates acid soils, but favours neutral to [[Alkali soils|alkaline soils]], and in some conditions it may be short-lived.<ref>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Lavandulae flos dried.jpg|Dried ''Lavandulae flos'' as used in herbal teas|thumb|upright=1.5]]
The flowers and leaves are applied in [[herbal medicine]].<ref name=pfaf>{{cite web|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Lavandula+angustifolia|title=''Lavandula angustifolia'' - Mill. |publisher=Plants for a Future |access-date=22 November 2020}}</ref> Commercially, the plant is used to produce [[lavender oil|lavender essential oil]] used in balms, salves, perfumes, cosmetics, and topical applications.<ref name="drugs">{{cite web |date=19 December 2022 |title=Lavender |url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/lavender.html |access-date=24 June 2024 |publisher=Drugs.com}}</ref> Lavender essential oil, when diluted with a carrier oil, is commonly used for [[massage therapy]] or [[aromatherapy]].<ref name=drugs/>

The flowers are also used as a culinary herb, most often as part of the North American version of the French herb blend called ''[[herbes de Provence]]''.

''Lavandula angustifolia'' is included in the [[Tasmania]]n Fire Service's list of low [[flammability]] plants, indicating that it is suitable for growing within a building protection zone.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Chladil and Sheridan|first1=Mark and Jennifer|title=Fire retardant garden plants for the urban fringe and rural areas|url=http://www.fire.tas.gov.au/publications/1709%20Brochure.pdf|website=www.fire.tas.gov.au|publisher=Tasmanian Fire Research Fund}}</ref>

===Hybrids===
''Lavandula'' hybrids are referred to as lavandins. Hybrids between  ''L. angustifolia'' and ''[[Lavandula latifolia|L. latifolia]]'' (spike lavender) are called ''Lavandula'' × ''intermedia''. They bloom later than the ordinary English lavenders.
